name: Uncovering Betrayal: About Anti-National Histories
description: About the LectureThe historian, much like Perseus, is expected to go on a quest to the archive, a repository of truth waiting to be discovered. But sometimes the archive gives up stories nobody went looking for: stories of deception, of broken loyalty, of comrades who turned.This talk recounts the history of Bhagat Singh's associates who reneged on the cause and betrayed their fellow revolutionaries. It then asks the uncomfortable questions: why bother with histories like these, and what does recounting them do for our present?The session explores:The little-told story of the revolutionaries who betrayed Bhagat Singh's circleWhat historians do when the archive contradicts the heroic narrativeWhy "anti-national" histories are worth recovering at allWhat remembering betrayal does to how we understand the presentAbout the SpeakerProfessor Aparna Vaidik teaches History at Ashoka University. Educated at St. Stephen's College, Cambridge University and Jawaharlal Nehru University, she has previously taught at Georgetown University, Washington DC, and the University of Delhi. She is the author of Imperial Andamans, Waiting for Swaraj and Revolutionaries on Trial, and of the creative non-fiction book My Son's Inheritance. She is actively involved in public pedagogy and is President Trustee of a charitable trust that runs a community library with more than 5,000 members. Although she writes about revolutionaries and militant protest in the British period, she encounters it every morning at home: she is the parent of two sassy and surly teenaged un-schoolers, one a trigger-happy radical and the other a brainy anarchist. When she isn't teaching or researching, her favourite pastime is couch-potatoing.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Whose Art Is It Anyway?
description: About the LectureJoin us for a participatory lecture that asks a question most of us never think to ask:Who gets to create, define and own art?Caste, class, religion, gender and sexuality shape who is allowed to create in the first place, whose work gets taken seriously, and how it travels once it leaves the maker's hands. Some forms are celebrated as "mainstream"; others are filed away as "folk", "obscene" or "political", those labels say more about the system than about the work.Drawing on narrative and performance practices across South Asia, theatre artist Sri Vamsi Matta looks closely at how artists from historically marginalised communities navigate spaces where their work is routinely appropriated, diluted or dismissed. This is about art as a living social practice, tangled up with identity, power and access.Expect discussion, examples and interactive prompts rather than fixed answers. The aim is sharper questions: what does it mean to witness art responsibly, where do we locate ourselves in relation to what we consume, and what changes when we see art not just as representation, but as a way of negotiating dignity, memory and justice?About the SpeakerSri Vamsi Matta is a Bangalore-based interdisciplinary theatre artist whose work is rooted in lived experience, political memory and anti-caste thought. Born into a Dalit community, his practice engages with the everyday and structural violence of caste, treating art as a space for refusal, repair and collective imagination. He works across theatre, performance, writing and participatory formats, bringing together autobiography, community history and radical pedagogy.His recent work Star in the Sky, on the emotional and political lives of Dalit students in Indian universities, was developed at Indian Ensemble's Idea Development Lab, shortlisted for the Sultan Padamsee Playwriting Award, and premiered in Bangalore in 2025. Come Eat With Me, a participatory performance examining caste through food and shared meals, has been performed nearly 50 times across India, the United States and Australia. He has taught and led workshops at UW–Madison, Northwestern University, Melbourne Law School, the University of Texas at Austin, Azim Premji University, Ashoka University and Mount Carmel College, among others.About Grounds for ThoughtGrounds for Thought is a series where unLecture, in collaboration with Blue Tokai brings researchers, artists and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does.

Along the way, we'll ask the question underneath all of it: what do we gain, and what do we lose, when we turn society into data?The session explores:How researchers use data and algorithms to detect polarization and media biasWhat happens to misinformation, hate speech and propaganda communities as they grow and change onlineThe techniques behind the field: NLP, machine learning, information retrieval and good old qualitative analysisWhat it means to study people at the scale of the entire web, and where that approach runs out of roadAbout the SpeakerAnirban Sen is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at Ashoka University. Before joining Ashoka in 2024, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Microsoft Research India, on the Technology for Emerging Markets team, where he studied misinformation, hate speech and propaganda communities on social media and how they evolve over time. description: Among Delhi's many historic cities, Jahanpanah remains perhaps the most elusive. Conceived in the fourteenth century as an ambitious attempt to unite earlier settlements within a single fortified capital, it was envisioned as a city without precedent. description: A FishMarket isn't a lecture. And yet an ordinary journey on foot, by bicycle, motorcycle or car routinely becomes an exercise in negotiation. The footpath disappears into parking. The pedestrian steps onto the road. The rider squeezes through a gap that probably shouldn't exist. The car stops wherever space appears. Each decision seems reasonable to the person making it. Together, they produce confusion, delay, and risk.But here's what we rarely ask: is this actually about bad civic sense? Or is it about a street that was designed without ever considering how people actually use it?This FishMarket will investigate how everyday disorder is created across the entire street. We'll will diagnose situations. We'll ask who or what shapes them. And then we'll move from diagnosis to solutions, examining which responsibilities belong to citizens, drivers, vendors, planners and authorities, and what changes in behaviour, rules, or design could actually help.Come ready to observe, challenge easy assumptions, and propose a better way for everyone to share the city.

name: Who Does the City Belong To?
description: Who Does the City Belong To?A conversation on public space and the lawYou have probably stood in front of a barricade this year. A road closed with no notice. A park gate locked at night. A station shut, a lane that used to be a shortcut now ending in a guard and a boom. Most of us have learned to route around it without thinking.But there’s a question underneath that almost none of us can answer: what are we actually entitled to in a public space and what happens when that space is closed, fenced or policed?In the first edition of The Human City Conversations, the urbanist Jagan Shah described a Delhi increasingly run by barricades and closures, and someone in the audience said that what privilege buys in this city is isolation. This conversation picks up exactly where that one stopped, because the next question is a legal one.We’ll ask what the Constitution actually gives us by way of a right to assemble and to protest. Whether a government can simply take a Jantar Mantar away. Whether there is such a thing as a right to walk in an Indian city, and who in Delhi really has it. And how much of what we call planning is in truth a question of who is expected to justify their presence in public, and who is not.It isn’t a lecture, and it isn’t a complaint session. It’s an hour of conversation, in plain words, followed by your questions put directly to someone who has spent two decades arguing these things in court.About the guestMihira Sood is a lawyer and scholar in the field of women’s rights, and practices at the Supreme Court of India and the Delhi High Court. She has taught at Jindal Global Law School and National Law University Delhi, and holds degrees from NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Columbia Law School, New York. She was among the youngest members to assist the Justice Verma Committee, whose recommendations reshaped India’s criminal law on sexual violence. She writes and speaks widely on women’s rights, feminist jurisprudence, equality law and civil liberties, and is a regular commentator in the national press. She has recently written a book Courting Equality which focusses on the Landmark Cases in the Battle for Women’s Rights (Juggernaut) traces fifty years of the law’s encounter with women’s lives — from the anti-dowry agitations of the 1970s, through Shah Bano and the Uniform Civil Code debate, to the Nirbhaya movement and its continuing reverberations, and on to the present backlash against the supposed misuse of these very laws.Copies will be on sale at Kunzum on the evening, at 20% off.About the seriesThe Human City Conversations is the live edition of The Human City Podcast, hosted by Ruchita Bansal, which for the past year has asked how Indian cities are planned, built and experienced — and who they are built for. name: Ghalib Aur Dilli : Poetry ,People & Lost Worlds
description: What happens when a poet's beloved city begins to disappear before his eyes?This is not a conventional Chandni Chowk heritage walk. Instead, we explore Old Delhi through the eyes, words and wonderfully complicated life of Mirza Ghalib—one of the greatest poets of the Urdu language.Ghalib loved Delhi, its culture, its people and its refined social world. But he also witnessed the city undergo extraordinary upheaval, particularly during and after the Revolt of 1857. As Delhi was devastated and its familiar world transformed, the poet found himself grappling with loss, uncertainty and the disappearance of a way of life he had known.Through his letters, poetry and anecdotes, we will explore how Ghalib saw his city, how he responded to its changing fortunes, and what his writings reveal about Delhi during one of the most turbulent periods in its history.As we walk through selected corners of Old Delhi, the city becomes the backdrop to his extraordinary story. The experience concludes at Ghalib ki Haveli in Ballimaran, bringing us closer to the poet, his world and the city that inspired him.Come for Ghalib's poetry, stay for his stories—and discover a very different way of looking at Old Delhi.

name: Body Language Speaks Louder Than Words@ThePianoMan
description: An OutClass Bar Lecture with Gaurav GillABOUT THE SESSION Every conversation has a second layer. Learn to notice it.Someone says they’re fine, but something feels off. A job candidate sounds confident, but their delivery tells a different story. A first date is going well — or is it? And what can a handshake, a fleeting expression or a change in posture actually tell you?We communicate even when we aren’t speaking. But how much can you really tell from the way someone looks, moves, listens and responds?Join Gaurav Gill, Consultant Psychologist and Body Language Expert, for an eye-opening evening that takes you inside the fascinating world of non-verbal communication. Drawing on real-world investigative experience, forensic psychology and high-stakes interactions, Gaurav will show you how to observe human behaviour with a sharper, more informed eye.What makes this especially interesting? The same principles of behavioural observation used in criminal investigations can also help us better understand everyday interactions — from first dates and friendships to job interviews, negotiations and workplace dynamics.WHO IS THIS FOR?The curious. The observant. The people who love figuring out what makes others tick.Whether you’re navigating dating, building your career, negotiating at work, studying psychology, or simply fascinated by human behaviour, this session will give you a fresh perspective on the conversations happening around you.No prior knowledge of psychology is needed. ABOUT THE SPEAKERFeatured on many podcasts, including Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, in an episode that has drawn more than 3.2 million views. Gaurav has trained law enforcement personnel and forensic professionals across India, including Delhi Police Crime Branch AHTU, CISF, RPF and GRP, and has delivered expert sessions at institutions including the National Forensic Sciences University and Rashtriya Raksha University. He was also featured on WION analysing world leaders’ non-verbal cues around the 2026 BRICS Summit.Now, he brings these insights out of the classroom and into the bar.WHAT YOU’LL DISCOVER• The face behind the words: Understand facial expressions, gestures, posture and eye movements — and what they may reveal about a person’s emotional state.• Nervousness or something else? Explore the difference between ordinary stress, discomfort and behavioural changes that deserve a closer look.• Can you spot a lie? Challenge popular myths about deception and discover why no single gesture can reliably tell you whether someone is lying.• Read the room: Recognise shifts in engagement, comfort and interaction during conversations, meetings and social situations.• Make a stronger impression: Learn how your own body language can influence how you come across in interviews, presentations, negotiations and everyday encounters.THE OUTCLASS EXPERIENCEWe believe the best conversations don’t always happen in classrooms.The OutClass brings powerful ideas and fascinating people into bars and cafés, creating a space where you can enjoy a drink, discover something unexpected and leave with more to think about — and talk about.Come for the drink. Stay for the thought.One evening. A new lens on human behaviour. And conversations that might never look the same again.
